# VeraJS

> A ~<!--size:app.kb-->7.0 KB<!--/size:app.kb--> reactive framework built on native web components. No build step required, no base
> class, no dependency arrays. Components are plain `HTMLElement` subclasses; templates are tagged
> template literals; state is a proxy that tracks what you read.

**This file is the complete API.** It is written to be pasted into an LLM context window — the whole
public surface is about 30 functions, so an assistant does not need training data on VeraJS to write
it correctly. Everything else is standard Custom Elements and tagged template literals.

If you already know lit-html the templates will look familiar, and the semantics are deliberately the
same — child-position values match it exactly, and `tests/lit-parity.test.mjs` measures that against
lit's own output rather than asserting it. VeraJS ships its own renderer and needs nothing from lit.

> ⚠️ **LIVING DOCUMENT — EXPECT DRIFT.** VeraJS is pre-release and under active development. The API
> is not frozen and this file will keep changing. It is maintained by hand, so it can fall behind the
> code. **When it disagrees with the source, the source wins.** Verify against
> `packages/*/dist/development/*.d.ts`, which is generated from the actual build.
>
> **Current facts (2026-08-31):**
> - All nine runtime packages are on npm: `@verajs/core`, `renderer`, `router`, `autoloader`,
>   `inserts`, `styles`, `store`, `jsx` and `ssr` — each release with a GitHub Actions
>   provenance attestation (`npm audit signatures`).
> - `@verajs/renderer` is browser-confirmed fastest-or-tied against lit-html on the benchmark's
>   eight operations; prefer it.
> - Render scheduling defaults to `requestAnimationFrame` (frame-aligned batching).
>   `setRenderScheduler(microtask)` gives Lit/Vue-style microtask flushing — it is what the
>   published DOM benchmarks use for like-for-like timing, and the right choice when update
>   latency matters more than frame alignment.
> - Tests: `node --test` + jsdom against BUILT artifacts, run twice — against the development build
>   and the production one — plus a browser layer on three real engines (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit)
>   under `@web/test-runner` and Playwright. Green in CI. `npm run gate` runs all of it.

---

## Mental model

Four things, and that is the whole framework:

1. `init(this)` in `connectedCallback` attaches VeraJS to a plain custom element.
2. `createStore(obj)` / `ref(v)` make state reactive. **Reading a property subscribes to it.**
3. `render(() => template)` re-runs whenever anything it read changes.
4. `useEffect(fn)` does the same for side effects.

There are no dependency arrays, no reactive-property declarations, and no base class.

## Minimal component

```js
import { init, createStore, render, html, wire } from '@verajs/core';
import { renderer } from '@verajs/renderer';

wire([renderer]); // once, at startup — see "Setup" below

class ClickCounter extends HTMLElement {
  connectedCallback() {
    init(this, { mode: 'open' });          // omit the options object for light DOM
    const state = createStore({ count: 0 });

    render(() => html`
      <button @click=${() => state.count++}>Clicked ${state.count} times</button>
    `);
  }
}
customElements.define('click-counter', ClickCounter);
```

## Setup — required once, before any component defines itself

```js
import { wire } from '@verajs/core';
import { renderer } from '@verajs/renderer';

wire([renderer]);       // what writes to the DOM. Core's `html` already produces what it accepts.
```

**Core ships no renderer.** `render()` with none registered paints nothing and warns once in
development, naming the two lines to add. Wire one at your app entry:

```js
import { wire } from '@verajs/core';
import { renderer } from '@verajs/renderer';
wire([renderer]);
```

Core's `html` needs no `setHtml` — it already produces the shape `@verajs/renderer` accepts, so the
one `wire` call above is the whole of the setup.

**Order matters.** A component that defines itself before `wire([renderer])` renders with nothing on
the `'render'` chain — `render()` warns once in development and draws nothing. Static
`import` declarations are **hoisted**, so this is wrong:

```js
wire([renderer]);
import './components/app.js';        // WRONG — hoisted, runs before wire()
```

```js
wire([renderer]);
await import('./components/app.js'); // correct — dynamic import is not hoisted
```

---

## `@verajs/core` — full export list

### Lifecycle

| Export | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `init` | `(element, shadowProps?) => void` | Call first in `connectedCallback`. Pass `{ mode: 'open' }` for shadow DOM; omit for light DOM. |

### State

| Export | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `createStore` | `<T>(obj: T) => Store<T>` | Deep reactive proxy. Nested objects are tracked too. |
| `ref` | `<T>(value: T) => { value: T }` | Deep reactive box for a single value. |
| `shallowRef` | `<T>(value: T) => { value: T }` | `.value` is tracked; **contents are NOT proxied**. Use for large immutable data such as list rows. |
| `untrack` | `<T>(fn: () => T) => T` | Read current state without subscribing. |
| `store._delete()` | `() => void` | Severs every subscription for an object store instantly. Non-enumerable; absent on primitive (`{value}`) stores. |
| `deps` | `(...values) => void` | Explicitly touch values to register them as dependencies. |

**Use `shallowRef` for lists.** Putting 1 000 row objects in `createStore` proxies all of them and
reading them back measures 20-30x the cost of a plain array (measured 2026-09-05; an earlier pass
said 60x, which the store has outgrown). If rows are replaced rather than mutated, `shallowRef` is
the right tool.

### Rendering

| Export | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `render` | `(template, ...args) => void` | Call inside `connectedCallback` after `init`. `template` is a function returning a template. **Required** — it is exactly `useRender(template)` followed by `mount()`. |
| `mount` | `() => void` | The same commit without a template, for a component whose whole job is a side effect. `init()` opens the setup and one of these two closes it: hooks registered between them do not run until it does. Calling `render()` bare still works and warns. |
| `svg` | tagged template | For content inside `<svg>`. The renderer parses it in the SVG namespace, which `html` cannot do — `document.createElement('circle')` yields an `HTMLUnknownElement` that never renders. |
| `mathml` | tagged template | The same, for content inside `<math>`. |
| `html` | tagged template | What you use. `setHtml` replaces it if you need a different tag. |
| `css` | tagged template | Returns `{ styleSheet, cssText }` for `static styles`. |
| `setHtml` / `setCss` | `(fn) => void` | Swap the template tags. |
| `wire` | `(module \| module[]) => void` | Install modules. From `@verajs/core` (re-exported from inserts). |
| `setRenderScheduler` | `(scheduler) => void` | Defaults to `requestAnimationFrame`. |
| `microtask` | `RenderScheduler` | Pass to `setRenderScheduler` for Lit/Vue-style microtask scheduling. |
| `useRender` | `(template, element, ...args) => void` | Lower-level; `render` wraps it. |
| `setStaticStores` | `(on: boolean) => void` | Server-only; `@verajs/ssr` calls it for `{ static: true }` renders — see the SSR section. In a browser it gives you a framework that does not update. |

### Props — passing data to a child component

**A parent binds properties; the child reads them off `this`. Nothing is declared on either side.**
No `static properties`, no props argument, no `declare`, no base class.

```js
// parent — any of these three spellings
html`<order-row .item=${row} .index=${i}></order-row>`          // template
html`<order-row ${props({ item: row, index: i })}></order-row>` // props(), from @verajs/renderer/spread
<order-row item={row} index={i} />                              // JSX — bare props ARE props on a dashed tag

// child — no declaration anywhere
customElements.define('order-row', class extends HTMLElement {
  connectedCallback() {
    init(this, { mode: 'open' });
    render(() => html`<p>${this.index}: ${this.item.label}</p>`);   // reading this.item TRACKS it
  }
});
```

`init()` **adopts** every bound property into a store-backed accessor, so a read in a render is
tracked and the parent's next commit re-renders the child. Values arrive **by identity** — an
array, a `Date`, a `createStore` store or a `ref()` stays itself and stays live, which is how a
child re-renders when the parent mutates the object it was given.

| Rule | |
| --- | --- |
| **Props are PROPERTIES, not attributes** | `item="…"` is an attribute and always a string. `.item=${…}`, `props({ item })` and JSX `item={…}` on a dashed tag are properties, any type, invisible to `getAttribute`. |
| **Lazy definition is safe** | A value bound before the child's module loads is recorded and re-applied by `init()`, repairing the ES2022 class-field clobber in both spellings. No `declare` needed for bound props. |
| **Defaults belong to the parent** | `props({ date: date ?? today })`, or read `this.date ?? today`. A class field default does not win — a bound value outranks it, which is what props mean. |
| **Your own accessors are kept** | A `get item()`/`set item()` pair receives through its setter and owns its reactivity (back it with your own store). A getter with no setter refuses the binding by name in development. |
| **SSR delivers them too** | `@verajs/ssr` hands the same values to the child's server render, so server and client render the same content. |
| **A key can arrive later** | A spread bag that grows a key on a live child is adopted reactively. Prefer stable shapes anyway (`props({ date: loaded ? date : null })`). |

Attributes are still the right channel for CSS hooks and static markup; `attributeChangedCallback`
is the platform's own and untouched by any of this.

### Effects

| Export | When it runs | Batching |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `useLayoutEffect` | before render (priority 25) | coalesced, microtask |
| `useEffect` | after render (priority 75) | coalesced, animation frame |
| `useSyncEffect` | immediately on every change (priority 75) | **not** batched |

All three accept `(callback, element?)` and **run a returned function as cleanup** — before the
next pass, and **on element removal** (no `disconnectedCallback` code needed; an author's own
`disconnectedCallback` still runs first if present):

```js
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(tick, 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);   // runs before the next pass
});
```

**Coalesced vs sync.** `useEffect` runs once per frame no matter how many writes landed, so it only
ever observes final state. `useSyncEffect` runs once per individual write and observes every
intermediate value — the Solid/Preact model.

```js
state.n = 1; state.n = 2; state.n = 3;
// useEffect     -> one run, sees 3
// useSyncEffect -> three runs, sees 1, 2, 3
```

⚠️ `useSyncEffect` **can infinite-loop** if it unconditionally writes state it also reads. Guard the
write or use `useEffect`. Development stops and names the recursion at depth 50.

⚠️ `useEffect` and templates can loop too, and there it is ambiguous — the default scheduler is an
animation frame, so an effect that writes what it reads runs once per frame, which is also how an
animation is written. Development **warns without stopping it** after 50 consecutive self-feeding
passes; production carries neither the counter nor the text.

| Export | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allowRenderLoop` | `(element) => void` | Marks a component's self-feeding loop as deliberate, silencing that warning for it. No-op in production. Throws in development if not given an element. |

The count is per element **and** per hook, and resets on the first pass that does not feed itself —
so a write scheduled from your own `requestAnimationFrame`, a timer or an event never trips it.

```js
init(this);
allowRenderLoop(this);
useEffect(() => { state.t = state.t + 1 });   // an animation, not a bug
```

### SVG and MathML

Content inside `<svg>` or `<math>` needs its own tag, because the namespace is decided when the
markup is parsed and cannot be fixed afterwards:

```js
import { html, svg } from '@verajs/core';

render(() => html`
  <svg viewBox="0 0 10 10">
    ${svg`<circle cx=${x} cy=${y} r=${r} fill=${color} />`}
  </svg>
`);
```

This is a TEMPLATE rule. In JSX the compiler picks the tag from the expression's lexical position —
shapes mapped in a list or built conditionally inside `<svg>` compile with `` svg`…` `` automatically.
`<foreignObject>`, `<desc>` and `<title>` all flip their content back to HTML; a top-level `<math>`
uses `` mathml`…` ``, but a `<math>` NESTED inside an `<svg>` stays SVG, exactly as the parser does.
So JSX authors never write the namespace tags by hand.

Shapes HANDED TO A COMPONENT work too, which lexical position alone cannot decide: in
`<Frame><path d="M0 0h24" /></Frame>` the `<path>` sits outside any `<svg>`, and the call site cannot
know what `Frame` renders. It does not need to — `<path>` is not an HTML element in any context, so a
template whose ROOT is an SVG-only name compiles with `` svg`…` `` wherever it was written. That covers
children passed directly, through a `<>…</>` fragment, and through a mapped list.

Three kinds of name are excluded, all conservatively — they fall back to previous behaviour rather
than mis-tagging. The ones SVG shares with HTML (`a`, `title`, `script`, `style`, `image`, `font`).
The ones that carry visible content as unknown HTML (`text`, `desc`, `tspan`, `foreignObject`,
`filter`, `mask`, ...), since the upgrade fires on the root tag alone and would otherwise turn
`<Box><text>hi</text></Box>` into a 0x0 SVG element. And the camelCase ones (`clipPath`,
`linearGradient`, `animateTransform`, ...), which a server emits verbatim and a browser parses
lowercased outside an `<svg>` — hydration would discard the server's markup and rebuild.

A root is never upgraded when a COMPONENT or CUSTOM ELEMENT lies in its children or an expression,
and never when an ATTRIBUTE carries JSX at all — a handler's template goes wherever the handler puts
it, which the shape around it cannot know. Upgrade is
spec-gated on the HTML namespace, so an SVG-namespaced one is permanently inert with no
`connectedCallback` and no diagnostic. `<foreignObject>`, `<desc>` and `<title>` are SVG's HTML
integration points and all three are exempt: their content parses as HTML there, so an element or a
component beneath one is safe and the shape around it still draws. The island's own ATTRIBUTES are
still checked, since those are emitted in the outer namespace.

The one shape an island cannot take is a STATIC element inside a `<title>`, which `@verajs/renderer`
scans as raw text in every template. An EXPRESSION never reaches that, so
`<g><title>{flag && <my-badge />}</title><path /></g>` upgrades and the badge still upgrades as a
custom element; only `<g><title><tspan /></title></g>` keeps the behaviour it had.

MathML's token elements (`<mi>`, `<mo>`, `<mn>`, `<ms>`, `<mtext>`) are the equivalent for CHILD
MODE — an expression inside one compiles `html`. They never exempt a root from refusal, because a
root is only ever upgraded to `svg`.

A SIBLING vouches for a name a root tag alone cannot prove. In
`<Frame><title>{label}</title><path d={d} /></Frame>` the children are separate roots, so `<title>`
— a name SVG shares with HTML — would be built as HTML inside the `<svg>` and be the accessible name
of nothing. One SVG-only name in the group settles it — an expression vouches through its own roots too, so a
mapped list of shapes counts, while one mixing namespaces does not — and the names excluded only for want of
context come with it (`title`, `a`, `style`, `script`, `image`, `font`, `text`, `tspan`, `desc`,
`metadata`, `switch`, `view`, `set`, `filter`, `mask`, `marker`, `pattern`, `symbol`). Alone they
are untouched, so `<Box><text>hello</text></Box>` stays readable text. The camelCase names stay out
even with a sibling, because their hazard is SSR casing rather than context. The vouch travels both ways: a sibling also settles
what an expression's own roots compile as, so `<Frame><path />{labels.map((t) => <text>{t}</text>)}</Frame>`
gives every `<text>` the group's namespace.

`@verajs/renderer` names an element committed into an `<svg>` or `<math>` in a DIFFERENT namespace
from its host, in development — HTML inside `<svg>` most often, but MathML inside `<svg>` and SVG
inside `<math>` are the same mistake, named by the same rule — but with different advice: HTML
content gets both remedies, while SVG-in-MathML and MathML-in-SVG are told only where to put the
root, because the template's tag is already right. It stays silent where the content
is correct: inside `<foreignObject>`, `<desc>` and `<title>`, inside MathML's token elements
(`<mi>`, `<mo>`, `<mn>`, `<ms>`, `<mtext>`), inside `<annotation-xml>` carrying an HTML
`encoding` or `image/svg+xml` (MathML's own registered spelling for an SVG annotation),
and for `<style>`/`<script>`, which never draw.

A HAND-WRITTEN template is the same story without a compiler to help: ``Frame(html`<path/>`)`` is
HTML, ``Frame(svg`<path/>`)`` is right, and development says so when it happens.

`html` alone would produce an `HTMLUnknownElement` named `circle`, which parses fine and never
renders. Bindings, keyed lists and in-place updates all work the same inside these tags.

### The signal argument

Every effect receives a signal describing what changed:

```js
useEffect((signal) => {
  signal.prop;       // name of the most recent change
  signal.value;
  signal.prevValue;
  signal.changed;    // Map<prop, { value, prevValue }> — everything in this batch
});
```

`signal.changed` is only present on coalesced runs, and holds each property's value at the **start**
and **end** of the batch.

### Extension

| Export | Signature |
| --- | --- |
| `wire` | `(descriptor \| connector \| array) => void` — a descriptor is `{ on, fn, priority, name? }`, **priority is required** |
| `inserts` | the registry `Map` |
| `connect` | optional on a descriptor — handed the registry before `fn` is registered, so a module that keeps none can be given core's |
| `createHook` | `({ callback, priority, element? }) => run` — build your own hook type. Returns the wrapped callback so a standalone value can drive its own first pass (`run(undefined, true)`), or `undefined` if registration was refused |

There is no reconciliation step. A module that would otherwise carry its own registry is handed
core's instead — `wire([router])` — which reads the same under a bundler and on a CDN page.
`connectInserts`, which replayed one registry into another, was removed in 0.2.0.

Insert points: `'render'`, `'init'` (an element was set up by `init()` — after its shadow root
exists, before its first render; this is how `@verajs/styles` attaches), `'proxy-handler'`
(property read — **what it returns becomes the value read**, so an observer must return nothing;
`undefined` and `null` leave the value alone), `'set-handler'` (property write, return `false` to
suppress default propagation), `'error'` (a hook threw), `'collection'` (a method read off a
`Map`/`Set` in a store — type-keyed, so plain-object reads never reach it; how
`@verajs/store/collections` attaches), and `'value'` (a child-position value the renderer has
no built-in answer for — return `true` to claim it; strings, numbers and nullish values never reach
it). `@verajs/inserts`' README documents each signature. `revision` (from `@verajs/inserts`) bumps
on every registration, so a reader may cache a chain against it.

⚠️ `wire({ on: 'proxy-handler', fn: () => count++, priority: 30 })` returns a number, so **every read of every store
yields that number** instead of the value. Write observers with a block body — `() => { count++; }`.

---

## Other packages

```js
import { initRouter, navigate, setMatchFunction } from '@verajs/router';
import { autoloader } from '@verajs/autoloader';
import { collections } from '@verajs/store/collections';
import { renderInto } from '@verajs/renderer';
import { keyed } from '@verajs/renderer/keyed';
```

### Collections (`@verajs/store/collections`)

Reactive `Map` and `Set` in stores. **Not in core since 0.2.0** — most stores hold plain objects
and every app was paying 367 B for it. Wire once at your app entry:

```js
import { wire } from '@verajs/core';
import { collections } from '@verajs/store/collections';
wire(collections);
```

Change detection is per method — `set` fires iff absent-or-different, `add` iff absent, `delete` iff
it returned true, `clear` iff non-empty. `get`/`has` subscribe per key; `entries`/`keys`/`values`/
`forEach`/`size` subscribe to every change, and so do `for…of` and spread. Reactivity is per entry,
not deep. `WeakMap`/`WeakSet` work.

Omit the wiring and core raises a development error naming the package the first time a collection
is read from a store, and the call after it throws — collection methods cannot run on a proxy.

### Styles (`@verajs/styles`)

`static styles` adoption. **Not in core since 0.2.0** — most apps do not use it and every app was
paying for it. Wire once at your app entry:

```js
import { wire } from '@verajs/core';
import { renderer } from '@verajs/renderer';
import { styles } from '@verajs/styles';
wire([renderer, styles]);
```

`styles` is the module; `adoptStyles` is the function it registers. `wire({ on: 'init', fn:
adoptStyles, priority: 50 })` is the same registration written out, for a non-default priority.

Shadow DOM gets constructed sheets on `adoptedStyleSheets` (or a `<style data-vm-sheet="styles">` for plain
strings); light DOM is hoisted to the document once per component class, wrapped in
`@scope (tag-name) { … }`. `applyStyles(styles, element)` is exported for manual use. Omit the
wiring and a component with `static styles` renders unstyled — core warns once, in development.

**Take `wire` from `@verajs/core`, never from `@verajs/inserts`.** A production `.min.js` inlines
the registry into every bundle, so registering through your own copy writes to a map core never
reads: it works in development and silently does nothing in production. This applies to any module
that registers an insert.

**`static styles` is not reactive, and does not need to be.** The sheet is adopted once — per
element for shadow DOM, per class ever for light DOM — and is shared by every instance of the class,
so reassigning `MyComponent.styles` does nothing and mutating the sheet would hit every instance.
What changes goes in custom properties: `var()` re-resolves whenever one changes, custom properties
inherit through the shadow boundary, and neither needs a re-adopt.

```js
static styles = css`p { color: var(--accent, blue); }`;
// …
render(() => html`<div style="--accent: ${state.accent}"><p>tinted</p></div>`);
```

### Keyed lists (`@verajs/renderer/keyed`)

```js
import { keyed } from '@verajs/renderer/keyed';
renderInto(html`<ul>${rows.map((r) => keyed(r.id, html`<li>${r.label}</li>`))}</ul>`, host);
```

Its own entry since 0.2.0: reordering is what makes lists expensive, most apps never do it, and the
algorithm is <!--size:keyed.gzip-->923 B<!--/size:keyed.gzip--> gzipped. Importing `keyed` is the entire installation — the marker stamps each
result with the strategy that reconciles it, so there is nothing to `wire()` and a list always names
its own reconciler. Additive like `/spread`: it imports nothing and works alongside `/hydrate`.

### Light-DOM slots (`@verajs/renderer/slots`)

`<slot>` works in a LIGHT-DOM component, with the platform's own semantics — so a component has ONE
version and its users write slot markup the same way either way.

```js
import { renderer } from '@verajs/renderer';
import { slots, slotted } from '@verajs/renderer/slots';
wire([renderer, slots]);

// <user-card><h2 slot="title">Ada</h2>a bio</user-card>
init(this);                     // light DOM — no shadow options
render(() => html`<article><header><slot name="title">Untitled</slot></header>
                  <main><slot>No bio.</slot></main></article>`);
```

Assignment follows the platform: `slot="x"` goes to the first `<slot name="x">` in tree order,
everything else (text included) to the first unnamed slot, duplicate names — first wins, and
fallback renders only while a slot has nothing assigned and comes back if it empties. In a SHADOW
root the module stands aside completely and the native `<slot>` renders untouched.

**`slotted(host, name?)`** is the accessor a component uses to read what its user gave it — native
assignment in a shadow root, the capture map in light DOM, so component code does not branch on
mode. `name` defaults to the unnamed slot.

⚠️ **`host.insertBefore(node, child)` throws once `child` has been distributed.** A light host's
children are MOVED into the slot they are assigned to, so a child you appended is no longer a direct
child of the host, and the platform refuses the insert with `NotFoundError` — where the same line
works on a shadow host, because nothing moves there. Use `child.before(node)` / `child.after(node)`,
which route through the node's current parent and are correct in both modes.

The `<slot>` ELEMENT is also still the component's handle on the slot, and means what it means in a
shadow root: **`@slotchange`** fires on first assignment and on every change (verified against real
shadow DOM, event for event — including for a slot whose rendering is currently displaced, since
assignment is independent of rendering). ⚠️ Bind it DIRECTLY (`@slotchange` on the slot): the
handles are out of the document, so the event cannot bubble and a host-level listener hears
silence. `node.assignedSlot` likewise answers `null` — the reverse lookup belongs to real shadow
trees; read forward through the slot handle or `slotted(host, name)`. Every one of these
boundaries has one cause — the shipped strategy removes the `<slot>` element — and the renderer
README carries a runnable ~50-line strategy that KEEPS it instead (`display: contents`, bubbling
`slotchange`, selectable slot), wired through the same public `'slot'` seam in place of `slots`; **`assignedNodes()`/`assignedElements()`** answer from the live
assignment through `event.target` or a `&ref`, with `{ flatten: true }` giving the SLOTTABLES of
the fallback currently on screen (a comment in fallback content is not one; a nested slot flattens
through to what it is showing); and **`name` may be a binding** — `<slot name=${section}>` routes by
the name it actually has and re-routes when it changes. Reach the element through `&ref` or
`event.target` only: it is deliberately not in the document, so `querySelector('slot')` finds
nothing and `isConnected` is `false`.

```js
html`<slot name=${section} @slotchange=${(e) => wire(e.target.assignedElements())}>Nothing yet</slot>`
```

The differences worth knowing, all deliberate:

- After distribution a slotted node's `parentNode` is inside the component's rendered tree rather
  than the host. That is what light DOM *is*, and it is exactly why the user's own CSS and Tailwind
  classes reach slotted content here when they cannot through a shadow boundary.
- **A `<slot>` cannot carry presentation here** — `class`, `style`, `id`. A light host has no second
  tree, so the slot element is not rendered and there is nothing for them to apply to; in a shadow
  root they do apply. Put them on a real element around the slot. Development builds warn, naming
  the attribute.
- A node added AFTER the first render joins its slot with full native semantics — bare text and
  attribute-less elements included, in document order. The renderer stamps everything it emits at
  a light host's top level with a hidden non-enumerable property, so an unstamped node there is
  knowably yours; `slot=""`/`slot="name"` still route, they are simply no longer required. Two
  notes: whitespace you append suppresses the default fallback, exactly as it does in a shadow
  root; and re-slotting a node (`slot="a"` → `"b"`) rejoins in LIGHT-TREE order, not arrival
  order — an item toggled into a "pinned" slot holds its place. What light has fewer of is
  POSITIONS you can name (a distributed child is no longer a direct child — see the insertBefore
  warning above), never worse ordering of the ones you can.
- `slotchange` only ever fires for a slot that HAS an assignment — here and in a shadow root alike.
  A component that must wire itself even when given nothing should do that once from a `useEffect`
  as well.

Opt-in and additive: `@verajs/renderer` carries only a small seam, and the module is
<!--size:slots.gzip-->3.34 KB<!--/size:slots.gzip--> gzipped. It works through SSR and hydration —
the server distributes and the client adopts the result in place, keeping node identity, so focus
and input values survive. Node-safe (it imports nothing and touches no global document).

### Spread (`@verajs/renderer/spread`)

⚠️ Spread REFUSES the injection sinks — `.innerHTML`/`!outerHTML`, `srcdoc`, and inline-handler
attribute names (`onclick`, any casing) — on client and server alike, because spread keys arrive at
runtime and lose the greppable-reviewable property the template spelling has. `on` + Capital with a
function is the event spelling and works. Need such a sink? Write it in the template.

Bindings whose names are not known when the template is parsed.

```js
import { spread } from '@verajs/renderer/spread';

render(() => html`<input ${spread({
  id: 'email',                    // attribute
  '.value': draft,                // property
  '?disabled': busy,              // boolean attribute
  onInput: (e) => handle(e),      // event — '@input' works too
})} />`);
```

Keys carry the same sigils as written bindings, so a spread key and a written binding mean the same
thing — including `&ref` for an element ref. A key that cannot be written into markup is **skipped**
(whitespace, a quote, `<`, `>`, `/`, `=`, a backtick, a control character); browsers accept some of
those and markup cannot carry them, so both sides refuse them rather than disagreeing.
`@verajs/renderer` costs 5 B for the protocol whether or not you install this; the package
is <!--size:spread.gzip-->1.60 KB<!--/size:spread.gzip--> and only apps importing it pay. Runtime is
at parity with writing the bindings out.

**Removing a key restores what the element held before the binding existed** — it does not remove
it. There is no value meaning "absent" for a property: `undefined` runs through coercing setters so
dropping `.value` would yield `""`, and `delete` cannot remove a prototype accessor. So
`<input type="text" ${spread({ type: 'number' })}>` reverts to `type="text"`. Bind `null` to remove.
On a hydrated page that restores the *server's* value, because a spread key replaces a static
attribute in server markup exactly as it overwrites one on the client — the original is gone by
construction. Bind `null` when you mean removal.

Several spreads on one element are fine; each element position owns its own keys.

**`props()` — a typed bag of PROPERTY bindings**, same entry point. One call in both surfaces:

```js
import { props } from '@verajs/renderer/spread';

html`<calendar-day ${props({ date, events })}></calendar-day>`   // template
<calendar-day {...props({ date, events })}></calendar-day>        // JSX — compiles to the same call
<calendar-day date={date} events={events} />                      // JSX — bare props ARE props on a component tag
```

Use it to pass a NON-STRING to a custom element — an array, a `Date`, a store — which an attribute
cannot carry. In JSX, bare props (rule 10 below) or the sigil spelling `.date={d}` do the same job;
props() is the bag TSX's type-checker is happiest with (`.date=` trips TS1003 there) and the one
that checks its keys against the element. Keys are property names, never sigils
(`props({ date })` binds `.date`); events and booleans keep their own spellings. Prefer keys
spelled conditionally — `props({ date: loaded ? date : null })` — over bags that change shape
(both work; a stable shape updates in place). With a type argument the bag is checked:
`props<CalendarDay>({ dat })` is a compile error naming the misspelling.

**Receiving props needs NO declaration.** A component that calls `init()` reads every bound
property off `this`, reactively: a render that reads `this.date` tracks it, the parent's next
commit re-renders, and a store or `ref()` passed down stays live (values arrive by identity). No `static properties`, no props argument, no `declare` needed — a value bound before
the component's module ran is recorded and re-applied by `init()`, so a bound value outranks a
class field default in both spellings (`item;` and `item = default`). Attributes are different:
`date="…"` is always a string in markup; props are properties. A class declaring its own
`get`/`set` pair keeps it — values arrive through the setter, and the pair owns its reactivity
(back it with your own store). Elements that never call `init()` (plain custom elements) get
properties written plainly, exactly as before. SSR included: a bound property reaches the child's
SERVER render too (by identity, never markup), so server and client render the same content from
the same data.

Keys are strings carrying sigils, so TypeScript cannot check them against the element — the trade
for names not known until runtime.

SSR serializes a spread: attributes, truthy booleans and — on form controls — the form properties
(`value`, `checked`, `selected`) reach markup; events are client state. A property on a rendered
COMPONENT tag is DELIVERED to that child's server render instead (written `.prop` and
`props()`/spread alike): the child SSRs from the same data its client render gets, the markup never
carries the property, and an unregistered dashed tag passes through for the client to handle.
Escaping stays in `@verajs/ssr`, in one place, exactly as for written bindings.

**The protocol is public.** A value at element position carrying `_$apply$(element, part)` applies
itself, and `_$attrs$()` lets it serialize server-side. Spread is the first user; any renderer
honouring the protocol can accept any implementation.

### Renderer (`@verajs/renderer`)

A keyed, template-identity renderer, <!--size:renderer.gzip-->4.57 KB<!--/size:renderer.gzip--> gzipped. `wire([renderer])` is the only wiring —
core's built-in `html` tag already produces the shape it accepts, so **no `setHtml` call is
needed** (lit-html templates also work, being structurally identical).

```js
import { init, createStore, render as show, wire, html } from '@verajs/core';
/** `renderer`, not `render`. The module is what `wire` takes; `render` is the function it registers. */
import { renderer } from '@verajs/renderer';
import { keyed } from '@verajs/renderer/keyed';
wire([renderer]);

// keyed lists: no repeat() import — key all items or none
show(() => html`<ul>${rows.map((r) => keyed(r.id, html`<li>${r.label}</li>`))}</ul>`);
```

Semantics that differ from lit-html — state these rather than assuming lit's:
- In a single-expression attribute, `null`/`undefined` REMOVE the attribute (there is no `nothing`).
- Keying is via `keyed(key, tpl)` on the result, not a directive.
- Element refs are element-position expressions: `<input ${myRef} />`. A function is called with
  the element; an object (including core's `ref()`) gets `.value` assigned. Runs once per distinct
  value.
- `hold(result)` preserves toggled-away DOM (lit's `cache`): form values and element state survive
  `html`<div>${hold(editing ? editor() : viewer())}</div>``.
- No other directives: no `classMap`/`styleMap` (build class strings, or a 3-line helper), no
  `until` (use state + an effect), no `guard` (reactivity already skips unchanged work), no
  `unsafeHTML` (use a `.innerHTML=${trusted}` property binding for trusted markup).
- A DOM node or DocumentFragment at a child position renders as itself, moved into place — how a
  template holds something another library owns (a charting canvas, a map container, an editor).
- Async values are not special: render a loading state and re-render from an effect.
- Plain strings render as TEXT, never parsed as HTML (there is no innerHTML sink).
- Child-position values match lit exactly: only `null`/`undefined` are empty. `false` and `0`
  RENDER, so `${cond && 'x'}` puts the word `false` on the page — write `${cond ? 'x' : null}`.
  `@verajs/ssr` serializes them the same way, so server and client agree.
- There is no `live()`. A property bound to a value it already holds is not re-applied, so a
  field the user has typed into keeps their text.
- The renderer owns its container below the mount point — do not hand-append siblings into it, and
  never call `Node.normalize()` on rendered content (child anchors are text nodes).
- Bindings inside comments are not supported (values consumed, ignored).
- **ARIA does not cross a shadow boundary.** `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby` and `<label for>`
  all match by ID, and IDs are scoped to their tree — so a page-level label cannot name a control
  inside `init(this, { mode: 'open' })`. No error, no warning, no accessible name. Three ways through:
  keep the relationship inside one template; put a role and name on the **host** with
  `ElementInternals` (`this.attachInternals()` before `init`, which does not clobber it); or use light
  DOM (`init(this)` with no second argument), where `static styles` still applies, hoisted per class.
  `delegatesFocus: true` forwards host focus to the first focusable child. All verified in Chromium,
  Firefox and WebKit — `tests/browser/aria-shadow-boundary.test.js`.
- `@event` accepts **both shapes `addEventListener` accepts** — a function (called with the element
  as `this`), or an object with a `handleEvent` method. The listener is registered once, so swapping
  the handler never churns the DOM. `undefined`, `null` and `false` mean no handler, so
  `@click=${enabled && onClick}` is a legal conditional binding; anything else that cannot listen is
  inert and named in development, because a listener is otherwise only validated when a user clicks.
- **Exit animations** need no framework support. Fade on `?hidden` with
  `.fade[hidden] { display: block; opacity: 0 }` — the `display: block` overrides the UA rule, and
  do NOT use `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` on `display`, which Firefox reports as supported
  and does not honour (measured). For a real removal, wrap the state change:
  `document.startViewTransition(() => flushSync(() => { state.rows = next }))`, where `flushSync`
  swaps the scheduler — `setRenderScheduler` returns the previous one for exactly this.
- **A dynamic tag name** needs `@verajs/renderer/tag`: `const H1 = tag\`h1\`` then
  `` html`<${H1} class="t">${x}</${H1}>` `` — note the `html` comes from that entry, not core. A
  string can never become a tag, only another tag. In JSX the same value is a component:
  `<H1 className="t">{x}</H1>`, with React's names mapped exactly as on a written element.
- **Stable shapes beat conditional swaps.** Rendering the same element every pass and toggling
  `hidden` is faster than swapping one subtree for another — template identity holds, so the
  renderer updates values in place instead of tearing down and rebuilding. Both forms are
  correct; this one is cheaper.

  ```js
  // fragile — two sibling parts, both swapping between a template and ''
  html`<section>
    ${items.length === 0 ? html`<p>empty</p>` : html`<ul>${rows}</ul>`}
    ${busy ? html`<p>loading</p>` : ''}
  </section>`

  // preferred — one shape, visibility toggled
  html`<section>
    <p ?hidden=${items.length > 0}>empty</p>
    <ul ?hidden=${items.length === 0}>${rows}</ul>
    <p ?hidden=${!busy}>loading</p>
  </section>`
  ```
- Hydration is a drop-in entry: SSR apps import from `'@verajs/renderer/hydrate'`
  (or point the CDN importmap's `@verajs/renderer` at `vera-renderer-hydrate.min.js`) — its
  `renderer` wirable binds the adopting render, so `wire([renderer])` stays the only wiring — and the
  first render ADOPTS server-rendered children — no per-part marker comments in server HTML
  (with light slots wired, the handoff is one offset attribute, one inert unassigned-content
  `<template>`, and a rare `<!---->` where two text runs would merge — each present only when
  needed, each consumed on adoption), node identity preserved, listeners attached, keyed updates
  move adopted nodes. Any
  mismatch is **repaired**: the result is always exactly what the template describes, and nothing the
  server sent survives that it does not — a stale attribute, a leftover element, corrected text.
  (It adopts and corrects where it can rather than clearing wholesale, so a partial mismatch still
  keeps most of the server's work.) Never mix the two entries in one app. The base entry
  carries zero hydration code.
- **Profiling (development only).** `@verajs/renderer/profiler` is another drop-in entry that
  re-exports the whole renderer API and adds measurement. It exists to make the rule above
  *visible*: it counts templates committed in place against templates that REPLACED a different
  template, which destroys and rebuilds the subtree while looking identical from the outside.

  ```js
  import { renderInto, profile, formatReport } from '@verajs/renderer/profiler';
  /** `profile` awaits an async driver — driving an app means awaiting frames. */
  const { report } = await profile(async () => { /* click around, await frames */ });
  console.log(formatReport(report));
  // 39 updated in place, 2 created, 19 rebuilt (32% of commits)
  // Template identity churn — these were torn down, not updated:
  //   10x  at body > main#app > ul.todo-list
  //       <li class="done"><s>${…}</s></li>
  //    -> <li><label><input type="checkbox">${…}</label></li>
  ```

  For live feedback while clicking around, `showProfiler()` mounts a panel in the corner and
  returns a function that removes it:

  ```js
  import { showProfiler } from '@verajs/renderer/profiler';
  const close = showProfiler();          // { corner, interval, rows } all optional
  ```

  API: `startProfiling()`, `stopProfiling(): ProfileReport`, `getReport(): ProfileReport`,
  `isProfiling()`, `profile(fn)`, `formatReport(report)` and `showProfiler(options?)`.
  `ProfileReport` carries `frames`, `ms`, `slowestFrameMs`, `updates`, `creates`, `rebuilds` and
  `churn[]` (`{from, to, count, where}`). The panel is plain DOM in a shadow root — it never
  renders itself through the renderer, so it does not appear in its own numbers.

  There is no production build of this entry, and there is nothing to strip from one: the
  renderer's instrumentation sits behind a `__DEV__` constant the build folds to `false`, so
  `vera-renderer.min.js` is byte-identical with and without it. Same rule as hydrate — never mix
  entries in one app.

### JSX / TSX (`@verajs/jsx`) — build-time, zero runtime

Opt-in, and **never required** — templates are the baseline. A hand-rolled parser compiles JSX into
the renderer's own tagged templates at build time, so what ships is `html\`…\`` with nothing added
to the bundle, and one JSX call site is one template call site (nested markup becomes inline
statics, so template identity and every renderer fast path hold).

```js
// vite.config.js
import { veraJsx } from '@verajs/jsx';
export default { plugins: [veraJsx()] };
```

```jsonc
// tsconfig.json — BOTH lines, and the second is the one people miss
{ "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "preserve",         // the plugin transforms JSX; `react-jsx` would emit _jsx() calls it never sees
    "types": ["@verajs/jsx"]   // loads the JSX namespace — without it EVERY element errors TS7026
} }
```

**Without `types`, TSX does not compile.** The namespace ships with this package's declarations, but
a TSX app imports `@verajs/core` and configures the plugin in `vite.config.js` — it never imports
`@verajs/jsx`, so TypeScript never loads them. The typings are permissive (every element accepts
every prop), so `key`, `onClick` and bare props all type-check; a fully typed per-element surface is
the known long tail, and the checked path for a component's props is `props<CalendarDay>({ … })`.

`.jsx` and `.tsx` are transformed, nothing else. Imports for `html`, `keyed`, `spread`, `svg` and
`mathml` are injected as needed (`inject: false` to provide them yourself; each is also individually
configurable — `html: ['h', 'my-lib']`).

**What it compiles to.** `onClick={f}` → `@click=${f}`; `className`/`htmlFor` → `class`/`for`;
`value`/`checked` → `.value`/`.checked` and `defaultValue`/`defaultChecked` → the attributes;
the boolean-attribute table → `?attr=${…}`; `key={id}` → `keyed(id, …)` on a list callback's root;
`ref={r}` → an element-position ref; `{...rest}` → `spread(rest)`;
`dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: h }}` → `.innerHTML=${h}`; `<Comp a={1}>kids</Comp>` →
`Comp({ a: 1, children: […] })`; `<>…</>` → the children; `<div />` and `<br></br>` are both
normalised to what the ELEMENT requires. The four renderer sigils pass through untouched in `.jsx`
— but **TSX cannot parse them** (`.date={d}` is TS1003), so in TSX write the bare prop or
`{...props({ date })}`.

**Two rules depend on position, and both are the reason this is not just a name table:**

- **On a dash-named tag, a bare prop is a PROP** — `<calendar-day date={d} count={3} active>` emits
  `.date=${d}`, `.count=${3}`, `.active=${true}`, delivered by identity and adopted reactively (see
  *Props* above). Carve-outs, both derivations rather than a list: a name that cannot be a JS
  identifier (`data-*`, `aria-*`, `xlink:href`) has no property spelling and stays an attribute, and
  `class`/`for` — the two names the DOM itself renamed — stay attributes (write `className`, as in
  React). None of the HTML-control guesses apply on a component: `disabled={x}` is its own prop.
- **A boolean CHILD renders nothing** — `{items.length > 0 && <em/>}` renders nothing when the test
  fails, React's rule. A hand-written template renders the word "false" there (lit's rule, which the
  renderer matches on purpose and names in development), so **this is the one value semantic on
  which JSX and a template differ**. Only booleans: `{0 && <x/>}` still renders `0`, as in React. A
  boolean INSIDE an array still renders — `{rows.map((r) => r.ok && <li/>)}` — because the filter
  sees the array, not its items; use `rows.filter(…)`.
- **Inside `<svg>`/`<math>`, expressions compile in that namespace** — a mapped or conditional shape
  becomes `svg\`…\`` (or `mathml\`…\``) automatically, `<foreignObject>` flips back to HTML. A
  function component compiles where it is DEFINED, so give an icon component its own `<svg>` wrapper.

**Refused with file/line/column** rather than passed to the next tool: a mismatched closing tag,
`key` anywhere but a list callback's root, children inside a void element, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`
in any other shape, an object `style`, a sigil with no value. Anything that does not parse is left
exactly as written, because `a < b` has to survive.

**Exports.** `veraJsx(options?)` is the bundler plugin; `transformJsx(source, fileName, options?)`
is the transform itself, for another bundler or a test; and `@verajs/jsx/standalone` exports
`runBlock(scriptElement)` for a `script[type="text/vera-jsx"]` block that arrives **after**
`DOMContentLoaded` — CMS content, a demo injected later — since blocks present at load run
automatically in document order. For no build at all, see **Buildless JSX — the whole recipe** below.

### Router

Three pieces make a routed app: an **outlet** (`<main view="main">`), **routed links** (a bare
`route` attribute), and the route list. `wire([renderer, router])` hands the router core's
registry, which is what makes it render — the router itself does not depend on core.

<!-- recipe -->
```js
import { wire, html } from '@verajs/core';
import { renderer } from '@verajs/renderer';
import { router, initRouter, navigate, currentRoute, resolve } from '@verajs/router';

wire([renderer, router]);

customElements.define('app-shell', class extends HTMLElement {
  connectedCallback() {
    this.innerHTML = `
      <nav><a route href="/">Home</a> <a route href="/users/7">A user</a></nav>
      <main view="main"></main>`;

    const appRouter = initRouter(this, { view: 'main' });   // 'main' matches [view="main"]
    appRouter.addRoutes([
      { path: '/', title: 'Home', component: () => html`<p>Home</p>` },
      { path: '/users/:id', name: 'user', title: (params) => `User ${params.id}`,
        component: (params) => html`<p>User ${params.id}</p>` },
      { path: '/*rest', title: 'Not found', component: (params) => html`<p>No ${params.rest}</p>` },
    ]);
    /** Guards run before the component; return false to cancel the navigation. */
    appRouter.on('before-route', () => true);
  }
});

document.body.innerHTML = '<app-shell></app-shell>';

await navigate('/users/7');
console.log(document.querySelector('[view="main"]').textContent);  // "User 7"
console.log(currentRoute().params.id, resolve('user', { id: 9 }));  // "7"  "/users/9"
```

`wire([renderer, router({ animate: true })])` — `router` is a dual — wraps every navigation's
render in `document.startViewTransition`: route changes crossfade, and elements named with
`view-transition-name` in CSS morph across pages. The initial render never animates, reduced
motion and unsupporting engines route instantly, and a throwing guard still rejects `navigate()`.

Routes support `path`, `name`, `title`, `component`, `action`, `children`, `view`, `redirect` and
`meta`.
`component`, `action`, `title` and `view` all receive `(params, to, from)` and may be `async`. Mark
links with a `route` attribute: `<a route href="/user/1">`. Render the outlet as
`<div view="main"></div>`.

Semantics worth stating:
- **Named routes**: give a route a `name` and build its URL with `resolve(name, params)` — values
  are encoded, an omitted `:tab?` takes its segment, a wildcard takes an array. `navigate({ name,
  params })` is the same call. Names are page-wide; a child registers its complete path. **A missing
  param fills from the current route**: from `/users/5/profile`, `navigate({ name: 'user-settings' })`
  goes to `/users/5/settings` with nothing threaded down. Explicit params win; an explicit
  `undefined` still omits an optional segment; with nothing routed yet the fill finds nothing.
- **Moving relatively** (a component that does not know where it is mounted): a SIBLING is a bare
  relative path — `navigate('settings')` from `/users/5/profile` — resolving exactly as
  `href="settings"` would (last segment replaced). The same place with a different view, or a
  CHILD, is `navigate({ name })` with params filled from here. Everything else composes from
  **`currentRoute()`**, which returns `{ path, query, hash, params }` page-wide — the pathname
  alone, a `URLSearchParams`, the `#fragment`, and params merged across every matched router; a
  copy, callable under Node, empty before anything commits — so `currentRoute().path + '/edit'`
  composes even when the current URL carries a query.
  One resolution rule, deliberately: relative `navigate()` and a relative href can never disagree.
  The one surprise — a relative word from a path ENDING in a param replaces it (`navigate('edit')`
  from `/users/5` is the sibling `/users/edit`, not the child) — is warned about in development,
  with both correct spellings named.
- `navigate(path)` is programmatic navigation — the trigger defaults to `'navigate'`. All routers
  on a page share the URL and all follow every navigation; history gets one entry per user
  navigation, none for back/forward or initial load.
- A newer navigation **supersedes** an older one. If a `component` or guard is still awaiting when
  the user goes somewhere else, the abandoned pass stops at its next checkpoint and commits
  nothing — no render, no history entry, no title.
- **Params are typed from the path** in TypeScript: `{ path: '/users/:id', component: (p) => p.id }`
  gives `p.id: string`, `*rest` gives `string[]`, `:tab?` gives `string | undefined`, and `p.nope`
  is a compile error — no annotation or codegen. A `path` function, and any route under `children`,
  keeps the loose `RouteParams` shape.
- A pattern token need not be a whole segment: `/fellow/john:id` matches `/fellow/johnXYZ`.
- **The most specific route wins**, not the first registered: static segment > required `:param` >
  optional `:param?` > `*wildcard`, summed over the pattern, so `/users/new` beats `/users/:id` and
  a catch-all sits last wherever it was declared. Same ranking as React Router. The score is read
  from the pattern text, so a `setMatchFunction` replacement is ranked by Vera's grammar rather than
  its own — register in the order you want if that matters.
- `children` **renders the whole chain**, outermost first, each level into an outlet the level
  above rendered. `/settings/profile` renders the `/settings` component into the router's outlet
  and the child into a `[view]` that component's own template rendered. A view name is resolved
  inside the level above, so a nested outlet may reuse the router's own name. If the parent renders
  no matching outlet the route does not apply (and warns in development).
- `beforeEnter` is a per-route guard, run after the router's `before-route` handlers and before
  `action`; return `false` to cancel. On a nested route the chain runs outermost first, so a parent
  can refuse before a child does any work.
- `alias: '/staff'` (or an array) makes other paths reach the same route, keeping whichever URL was
  used. Relative to the parent, exactly as `path` is.
- `router.removeRoute(name)` takes a named route and its aliases back out; `router.deleteRouter()`
  removes the router entirely.
- `back()`, `forward()` and `go(n)` are exported alongside `navigate`.
- Relative hrefs on routed links resolve **as the browser resolves them** — from `/docs/intro`,
  `href="edit"` is `/docs/edit`, NOT React Router's `/docs/intro/edit`. A cross-origin href is left
  to the browser. Resolution goes through `document.baseURI`, which is what the platform uses, so a
  `<base href>` on the page moves routed links exactly as it moves every other link.
- **Serving from a subdirectory:** write routes at the root (`/users`, not `/app/users`) and call
  `setBasePath('/app')`. The router adds the base when writing to the address bar, strips it when
  reading one back, and marks a link written `href="/app/users"` active on `/users` — and nothing
  else about the page changes. A `<base href="/app/">` element works too (the router reads it;
  `setBasePath(null)` returns to reading the document), but a `<base>` re-points EVERY relative URL
  on the page — assets, form actions, and relative `navigate()` alike — so `'settings'` then means
  `/app/settings` from anywhere rather than the sibling of where you are. Platform-correct, and why
  `setBasePath` is the default advice. `navigate` accepts either
  spelling. **Write hrefs relative or with the base** — a route-space `href="/users"` works when
  clicked (the router re-bases it) and is a broken URL in a new tab or when copied; development
  builds warn and name the href you should have written. `resolve(name, params)` returns the MOUNTED
  path, so it is `href`-ready, and `navigate()` accepts it unchanged.
- Params arrive **percent-decoded**: `/u/John%20Doe` yields `John Doe`, and each wildcard segment
  decodes individually. A malformed escape yields the raw text rather than throwing.
- Window listeners attach on the first `initRouter`, so importing the router is side-effect-free
  and Node-safe (SSR can import it; routing itself is browser-only).
- **`@verajs/renderer` is NOT Node-safe** — it captures `document` at module scope, so importing it
  where there is no DOM throws `ReferenceError: document is not defined`. Same for
  `@verajs/renderer/hydrate`, `/profiler` and `@verajs/jsx/standalone`. Node-safe: `core`,
  `inserts`, `store`, `store/collections`, `renderer/keyed`, `renderer/slots`,
  `renderer/spread`, `renderer/tag`, `router`, `styles`, `autoloader`, `jsx`, `ssr`. In a universal app pass the
  renderer in as a parameter rather than importing it from shared code.
- Routed links must live in the router's own template — links inside a child component's shadow
  root are invisible to the click listener (event retargeting).
- A `before-leave`/`before-route` handler returning `false` cancels navigation; a **throwing**
  handler also cancels (fail-closed). `after-route` is cleanup only and cannot cancel. Every
  handler runs even after one cancels, and the results aggregate.
- The three events are also dispatched as DOM events on the router element — `vera:before-leave`,
  `vera:before-route`, `vera:after-route` — bubbling and composed, with
  `{ currentRoute, previousRoute }` on `detail`. `preventDefault()` on either `before-` event
  cancels the navigation, exactly as returning `false` does.
- Pattern metacharacters are literal: `/file.html` matches only that path. `:param`, `:param?`
  (optional — the segment and its slash may both be absent) and `*rest` are the only special
  tokens. An optional param that did not match is absent from `params`.
- `meta` is arbitrary data the router carries but never reads; it arrives on every snapshot as
  `to.meta`, which is where auth flags, layout names and analytics ids belong.
- `router.currentRoute` is where that router is now — the snapshot, with params and query already
  parsed — or `undefined` until it has routed once.
- Hash fragments: the fragment is on every snapshot as `to.hash` (`#` included). A hash-only change
  does not re-route — the route did not change — but each router's `currentRoute` takes the new
  fragment and `after-route` fires with `trigger: 'hashchange'`. `path#hash` navigation costs one
  history entry, scrolls to the anchor, and sets `:target`; deep-linked anchors scroll after the
  initial route renders. `navigate(path,
  'replace')` swaps the current entry. With `pushHash: false` fragments never reach
  the URL — they go to `hashChangeFunction` only.
- Redirects: `{ path: '/old', redirect: '/new' }` or ``redirect: (params) => `/user/${params.id}` ``.
  Resolves before anything renders; the abandoned path costs no history entry; chains cut off
  after 10 hops.
- Guards are the event system: `router.on('before-route', (to) => to.params.id !== 'x')` — return
  `false` to cancel. For auth-style redirects, `on('before-route', ...)` + `navigate('/login',
  'replace')` is the pattern.
- Query strings never reach pattern matching (`/users?page=2` matches `/users`); the parsed
  `URLSearchParams` is `to.query` on every snapshot.
- Clicks with modifier keys, other buttons, `target`, or `download` are left to the browser.
- Active links: exact match gets `.active` + `aria-current="page"`; ancestor links (`/users`
  while at `/users/5`, segment-boundary, root excluded) get `.active-within`.
- Scroll: fresh navigation lands at top; back/forward restores the position the user left that
  entry at (the router stamps it into history state and restores after content renders).
  `initRouter(el, { scrollBehavior: (to, saved) => … })` replaces both — `saved` is the stamped
  position on a `popstate` and absent otherwise.

### Autoloader

```js
wire([autoloader(import.meta.url, 'components', { extension: '.js' })]);
```

Fetches `components/<tag-name><extension>` the first time an undefined element appears inside an
element carrying the `data-autoload` attribute. Use `extension: '.ts'` in a TypeScript dev server.
`componentsDir` is optional — omit it for components beside the entry file.

Semantics worth stating:
- Discovery is **observed, not polled**: a marked component is watched once with a
  `MutationObserver`, so an element is found whenever it enters the DOM — by a render, by
  `innerHTML`, by a third-party widget, or by being in the HTML file already. Creating an
  `autoload()` scans the page on demand, so hand-written static markup works with nothing rendering.
- Watching is **per-component opt-in**: each component hosting lazily-loaded children needs the
  `data-autoload` attribute. All three attributes are watched, not read once — marking a component
  `autoloader` later reaches inside a shadow root it already had, repointing `data-autoload-dir` retries
  from the new location, and removing `data-autoload-ignore` lets an element load.
- Server-rendered pages work: `autoload()` reaches through declarative shadow DOM, so components
  inside `<template shadowrootmode="open">` load with nothing rendering. An observer cannot cross into a descendant's shadow root, so that child
  marks itself (Vera components are offered up automatically by the `'render'` insert).
- `data-autoload-dir="alt"` overrides the directory per element; it must resolve **inside the entry
  file's directory** — absolute URLs, `//host`, and `../` escapes are refused. (It is
  `data-autoload-dir`, never HTML's global `dir` attribute.)
- One load attempt per URL per page load, and one module per **tag** — `<x-y>` and
  `<x-y data-autoload-dir="alt">` are two URLs for one tag, and a tag can only be defined once. The
  second location is tried only if the first fails.
- A failed load dispatches `vera:autoload-error` on the element (bubbles, composed,
  `detail: { tag, src, error, element }`) as well as logging, so an app can render a fallback.
- `autoloader` returns ONE function with three shapes: `autoload()` scans the page for
  `[data-autoload]` hosts, `autoload(element)` watches that component, `autoload(shadowRoot)` watches
  that root (no attribute — handing it over is the opt-in, and the only way into a component that
  never marked itself). Creating an autoloader has no side effects; `autoload()` is what makes
  hand-written static markup work, and can be called again whenever new markup lands.
- It carries `url(tag)` — the absolute URL it would fetch, for warming with `modulepreload`, a
  prefetch, a service worker, or just to answer "why that URL?" — and `retry(element)`, which
  forgets that element's tag failed and tries again.
- `data-autoload-ignore` excludes that element only, not its subtree.
- `resolve: (tag, dir) => url` replaces URL building for a layout `dir/tag.ext` cannot express
  (`tag/tag.js`, `tag/index.js`). The result is still bounded by the entry file's directory.

### Reactive collections — semantics (`@verajs/store/collections`, wired above)

```js
const state = createStore({ tags: new Set(), users: new Map() });
state.users.set(id, user);   // re-renders subscribers of that key (and of size/iteration)
```

Semantics worth stating (the wiring requirement is in the Collections section above — this does
NOT work without `wire(collections)`):
- `get`/`has` subscribe per key; `size`, `entries`/`keys`/`values`/`forEach`, `for…of` and spread
  all subscribe to every change.
- No-op mutations are silent: `set` with the same value, `add` of an existing member, `delete` of
  a missing key. `clear` notifies every previous key plus the global channel.
- Reactivity is **per-entry, not deep**: values returned by `get` are raw, so mutating
  `map.get(k).x` is untracked — replace the entry instead. `'_global'` is the reserved
  every-change channel key (exported as `GLOBAL`).
- Method identity is stable (`map.get === map.get`), and chained calls (`set().set()`) stay
  tracked.
- **`WeakMap` and `WeakSet` are reactive too**, per key, and hold nothing: their dependencies are
  stored in a `WeakMap`, so a tracked key is still collected once you drop it. They have no `size`
  and no iteration, so only `get`/`has` subscribe and only `set`/`add`/`delete` notify.
- **`Date` and `RegExp` are not proxied**, in Vue either. Their methods read internal slots, so a
  bare proxy throws (`this is not a Date object`), and reactivity would mean wrapping every mutator
  for a case whose idiom is replacement. `state.when = new Date(t)` is a property write and fully
  reactive; `state.when.setTime(t)` is not. This is core's rule, and applies with or without the
  collections module.

---

## `@verajs/directives` — behavior as attributes

Attribute-activated behavior for markup nobody writes JavaScript for: the adjectives to the
component system's nouns. Prefix `data-vd-`. **Nothing is wired by default** — the engine ships no
vocabulary, and each pack is additive and imports nothing from the engine.

Not published yet (`private: true`, 0.0.0). Entries: `@verajs/directives` (everything, wires
nothing) · `/core` (engine, core external) · `/standalone` (engine + its own store, for pages with
no vera) · `/interaction` `/expressions` `/motion` `/query` `/remote` (packs).

```js
import { wire } from '@verajs/core';
import { renderer } from '@verajs/renderer';
import { wireDirectives, directives, interactions, expressions } from '@verajs/directives';

wire([renderer, directives]);          // `directives` is core's connector — activation per component
wireDirectives([expressions, ...interactions]);
```

`wire([directives])` is correct in a browser AND under `@verajs/ssr`: the connector chooses its
insert point per runtime (`'init'` in a browser, `'settle'` on a server). Guard your RENDERER
wiring for SSR, never your directives wiring.

**Engine API.** `wireDirectives(descriptorOrConnector | array)` · `activate(root)` /
`deactivate(root)` (any root, shadow roots included — closed ones too, via a component's `init`) ·
`settled(): Promise<void>` (test/e2e primitive) · `rejections(el?)` (every refusal:
`{ element, directive, code, message, fix }`) · `describeDirectives()` (the live vocabulary — build
GUI panels from this, never a hand-written list) · `wireActions({ name: fn })` /
`describeActions()` · `describePayloads()` (the `$` vocabulary per
event base — the other half of that list) · `wirePayloads({ base: { name: getter } })` · `stateOf(el)` (what this element can SEE,
resolved per key up the carrier chain exactly as its directives resolve — live, and writable
through the same owner rules) · `renderDirectives(root)` (server; returns nothing) and
`takeDirectiveNames()` (server; the one door to the names, unclaimed ones included, which are what
to preload).

**Value classes**, declared per directive and applied BEFORE the directive sees the value:
`literal` (raw text; a bare word is a string, never a state read) · `expression` · `object` (a
braced object whose VALUES stay lazy — evaluate them with `ctx.eval`, which is what lets a config
key read state) · `none`.

**Event payloads — the `$` namespace.** A handler reads the event that ran it through declared
variables: `data-vd-on-input="{ q: $value }"`, `data-vd-on-click="{ x: $x }"`,
`data-vd-on-keydown-enter="{ go: true }"`. Bases and their variables (generated — do not hand-edit):

<!--payloads-->
- every base — $type
- `click`, `dblclick`, `mousedown`, `mouseup`, `mousemove`, `contextmenu`, `pointerdown`, `pointerup`, `pointermove` — $x $y $button $type
- `keydown`, `keyup`, `keypress` — $key $type
- `input`, `change` — $value $checked $type
<!--/payloads-->

Values are
PRIMITIVES, never the event: native properties live on prototypes, so reaching for them would hand
attribute text the whole DOM API. Register a base with `wirePayloads({ 'my:event': { n: (e) => e.detail.n } })` — NAME → getter, so a
base cannot declare a variable it never reads; read the vocabulary with `describePayloads()`. An
unknown `$var` REFUSES THE WHOLE HANDLER, in both builds — writing `undefined` under the author's
key is a working page with wrong behaviour — and says what the event does offer.

The class TYPES what `apply` and `ssr` receive: `Directive` is discriminated on `value`, so
`value: 'object'` gives `apply` a `ParsedObject` of unevaluated entries and using one as a finished
string is a compile error, not a bug report. `ValueOf<K>` is exported for a helper that needs to
name one.

**interaction pack.** `state` (engine-owned; seeds a subtree store, initials are expressions in
declaration order) · `show` · `class` · `style` · `text` · `bind-*` (false/null/undefined removes,
true is present-empty; `value`/`checked`/`selected`/`open` write the live property; `href`/`src`/
`srcdoc`/`style`/`class`/`on*` are refused) · `on-*` (delegated: one root listener per event type,
so swapped-in markup works from its first event; members `on-keydown-enter`, `on-outside-click`,
`on-escape`, `on-window-*`, `on-document-*`, `init`, `on-submit`, `on-submit-native`) · `sync` ·
`persist` · `every` · `focus-on` / `focus-trap` / `focus-return` · `doc-class` · `scroll-lock` ·
`copy` · `scroll-to` · `watch`.

**`wireActions({ name: fn })`** — the named escape hatch for the 1% the grammar cannot express.
An action is INVOKED by name from a handler value, never written inline:
`wireActions({ checkout: (ctx, event) => api.checkout(ctx.get('cart')) })` with
`data-vd-on-click="{ res: checkout() }"`. It receives `(ctx, event, ...args)` — arguments come from
the expression, so `slug(title)` passes state in and its RETURN is assigned. Actions run ONLY while
a handler is firing: in a reflection they refuse (`action-outside-handler`), because a reflection
re-runs whenever its inputs change and would fire the action every time. `describeActions()` lists
the registry, which is what makes "what JavaScript can this page run" a question with an answer.

`watch` (object) runs assignments when a state key CHANGES — `data-vd-watch="{ q: { page: 1 } }"`.
It does not fire on the first pass, so a shared link's `?q=ber&page=3` survives; and it is for
changes you did NOT author (a link, a fetch, another component). Where you wrote the handler, put
the reset in it: `{ q: $value, page: 1 }`. A watch that writes a key it watches is stopped with
`watch-loop`.


**expressions pack** — optional tier, CSP-safe (no `eval`, no `Function`). Comparisons (`==` is
STRICT; writing `===` is refused with a teaching message), arithmetic, ternaries, `!`, and PURE
functions only: `abs min max round floor ceil len upper lower`. Calm math: `undefined`, `NaN` and
division by zero render rather than throw, and `!missing` is the absence idiom.

**State addressing.** A read resolves to the NEAREST ancestor that OWNS the key (crossing shadow
boundaries host-ward); `@key` is the page-global store. `@route` is published by the query pack.

**motion pack** — one attribute, `data-vd-motion`, taking a preset name (`fade-up`, `zoom-in`, …
from a WIRED pack — see below) or an object with **two halves**: properties inside `keyframes`,
settings outside it. (The engine underneath is `@verajs/motion` — its own package with lean
embedder entries `./core` `./ssr` `./client` and the `vera-motion-emit` CLI; a vera page never
installs it directly, the pack carries it.) —
`data-vd-motion="{ keyframes: { opacity: '0% 0, 100% 1', translate-y: '0% 40px, 100% 0px' },
scroll: '70%, 50%', inertia: 0.2 }"`. The split is what makes `%` unambiguous: inside `keyframes` it is
**progress along the animation**, outside it a **position on the screen** (`0%` top, `100%` bottom,
like CSS `top:`). Progress is how far the element has travelled UP through its range — `0%` just
arriving at the bottom, `100%` just leaving at the top, which is the direction CSS `view()` runs.
A property written at the top level, or a setting written inside `keyframes`, is refused by name
with the move spelled out. Keyframes are `'progress value'` pairs; a lone value is the end. **A list
of lone values is a sequence spread evenly** — `'0, 1'` is `'0% 0, 100% 1'` and `'0, 1, 0, 1'` is
0%/33.333%/66.667%/100%; one explicit position anywhere turns that off. **A missing `0%` or `100%`
frame comes from the ELEMENT'S OWN VALUE, exactly like CSS `@keyframes`** — that is why a lone value
works at all (`opacity: '0.2'` is one frame at 100%, animated to from wherever the element is).
Write the stop to hold instead: `'0% 0, 50% 0, 80% 1'`. **One current exception, being reviewed:**
properties sharing an easing are compiled into one `@keyframes` rule, and a property that stops
short of an end takes its own first/last value there rather than the element's when another property
in that group reaches it — so `{ opacity: '0.2', scale: '0, 1' }` pins opacity at `0.2` throughout
while `{ opacity: '0.2' }` animates. Writing the stop (`opacity: '0% 1, 100% 0.2'`) is exact in
every case and is the reliable form. **One malformed entry refuses the whole
property by name** — the other properties on the element still animate, and nothing is re-timed
around the hole. **Over 256 stops the list is refused** rather than truncated, since a truncated
list is a different animation nobody wrote.
Per-property easing uses the nested form `{ frames: '…', ease: '…' }`. Width bands merge over the
base, by registered name or literal range (`'…; [mobile]: …'`, `'…; [0-560]: …'`); the names come
from `motion({ breakpoints })`, which is JavaScript, never an attribute. **`scroll` names where the animation begins and ends;
scrubbing spreads it across that span, playing runs it at each end.** Each half is
`'<edge> <screen position>'` or ONE token for the leading edge, comma-separated —
`scroll: '70%, 50%'` is a fixed 40% of the screen whatever the element's height, where the defaults
(`'start bottom'` → `'end start'`) scale to its own transit. A comma is required: `'70% 50%'` is
already a legal single alignment.

**`play` (SECONDS, like `inertia`) makes it a playthrough instead of a scrub** — crossing a threshold
runs the keyframes over time. Where transitions can express the value (the common from→to shapes),
play compiles to CSS TRANSITIONS — the compositor owns the clock, and reversing mid-flight follows
the platform's reversing algorithm (from the current value, retimed — faster than the forward run,
and a y>1 curve may reverse-overshoot). Everything else (multi-stop pulses, `progress`/`tick`
riders, width bands, mixed-shape composites) keeps the linear ramp; the dispatch is compile-time
and has no authoring surface. One `scroll` half is one line crossed both ways (in going down, out
coming back up past it); two halves are an entrance and an exit. `run-once` latches after the first
play. `play` beside `inertia` is refused (same transition); `ease` composes with a play — the clock is
linear over `play` seconds and the easing reshapes each segment as it is swept, so
`keyframes: { scale: '0% 0, 100% 1' }, ease: 'ease-in-out', play: 0.6` reads exactly as written. **`when: '.selector'` GATES** — it animates while matching and
rests at its start otherwise; `when` + `play` is a UI transition. **`anchor` measures against ANOTHER
element** — `anchor: '#section'` (found with `querySelector`), `anchor: 'closest(.card)'` (the element
ITSELF or its nearest matching ancestor — `Element.closest`, which is inclusive and stops at a shadow
boundary), or `anchor: 'self'` (the element's own transit). Use `closest()` in repeated markup: with a
plain selector every copy resolves to whichever the document puts first. A selector LIST is refused
for the plain form and allowed inside `closest()` — `querySelector('.a, .b')` silently means
"whichever is first in the document", `closest('.a, .b')` means "the nearest ancestor matching
either". **`pointer: 'x' | 'y' |
'distance'` drives the SAME timeline by pointer position instead of scroll** — `x`/`y` track the
viewport (or the `anchor`'s box), `distance` is euclidean from the scope's center over its
half-diagonal, clamped so leaving scope reads exactly 1. A SOURCE CHAIN falls back:
`pointer: 'x, scroll'` uses x on a fine hover-capable pointer, scroll otherwise, and where
NOTHING is available the variable holds the first source's rest value (x/y 0.5, distance 1) —
design keyframes so rest is the finished pose, and the page is complete on touch by default.
`inertia` composes (the mouse-follow feel), and so does `play` — a pointer-sourced play sweeps
to each pointer position over `play`-proportional seconds; the `scroll` SETTING and `stagger`
beside `pointer` are refused by name. The generated CSS is identical to scroll's: the pointer never joins the
hash, so both drivers share one rule. `stagger` goes on the PARENT, and
is refused with `play` until a per-sibling time delay exists. `inertia` smooths the value toward its
target, the one thing CSS scroll-driven animation cannot do — that is a pure function of scroll
position. **`progress: '--p'`** writes the timeline position to a custom property so CSS can read it
(opt-in; one write per element per frame), which is how anything outside the animatable-property
table — gradients, shadows, `clip-path` — gets animated. **`function: 'name'` hands the same number to a
registered JavaScript function** — `wireFunctions({ name: (el, p) => … })` from page code — for what CSS
cannot do at all: a canvas, text content, WebGL. The attribute NAMES a function and never contains
one, `tick` may be the whole animation (no `keyframes` needed), and a throwing tick is disabled for
its own element and reported, never the page. The escape hatch, not the road — it is a per-frame JS
call, so prefer `keyframes` or `progress` wherever CSS can express the effect.
**First frame everywhere** — the page is designed complete and motion derives from it, so the
first frame can be server-made in ANY stack: vera SSR calls `renderMotion(document, { wire })`
(host-agnostic — jsdom at build works for Astro/Next/Eleventy/anything); static HTML gets
`npx vera-motion-emit dist/**/*.html` (jsdom as a devDependency), which post-processes built
files through the same pipeline; buildless pages either load the script as a BLOCKING tag at the
end of `<body>` (beats first paint on most pages), opt into `data-vd-cloak` (hidden until
activation), or accept a cosmetic flash — cosmetic because the resting page is complete by
design. Reduced-motion visitors always get the designed page: emitted `@media
(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` blocks neutralise seek animations and pin transition-mode
plays to their END state — no driver involvement, so it holds with JavaScript off too.
`data-vd-motion-group` on a container makes a region (own axis, scroller, defaults).
**Server diagnostics reach the browser, because the author is not at the server's terminal**:
`renderMotion` returns `problems`, and on an SSR-ONLY page (no hydration, so no client scanner ever
runs) that array was the only copy — read by a server process, never by the person who wrote the
value. It now also emits one inline `<script data-vm-diagnostics>` that `console.warn`s every problem,
gated on `diagnostics` (default: `NODE_ENV !== 'production'`; pass `false` to be certain, `true` to
force it in staging). Pass `nonce` if the page sets a CSP nonce — **without one a strict `script-src`
blocks the channel silently, which reads exactly like a page with no problems**. A clean page emits
no script at all.
**Inline delivery — the cache-escape hatch**: `motion({ inline: true })` client-side and
`renderMotion(doc, { inline: true })` server-side deliver each element's generated CSS as its own
`<style data-vm-sheet="inline">` child instead of the shared sheet, so a cached/replayed fragment
carries its rules. Costs (stated, deliberate): duplicate rules across same-hash elements, a
`:first-child`/`:nth-child` shift inside the element, and `@property` never rides inline
(document-global — the wire registers it via JS; no-JS seek is correct untyped). Hydration takes
matching children over in place.
Vocabulary modules extend the object's KEYS, never the attribute space: `paint`
(background/color/border-color/shadow/text-shadow), `path`, `sequence` (a tick consumer:
`function: 'sequence'` scrubs an image sequence onto a `<canvas>`, configured by `frame-*` settings), plus
